articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) has tightened its validation of technical descriptions in budget documents after errors were flagged in project information, including coordinates for proposed…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agriculture (DA) has tightened its validation of technical descriptions in budget documents after errors were flagged in project information, including coordinates for proposed farm-to-market roads (FMRs).

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. ordered a continuing review of project descriptions, supporting documents and validation procedures to ensure that information submitted by the agency is accurate, complete and technically verifiable.

This came after civil society groups such as the People’s Budget Coalition, BetterGov.ph and BistoProyekto flagged discrepancies in the FMR coordinates submitted by the DA during the Senate hearing for its budget for 2027.

An initial review of the discrepancies were traced to encoding and typographical errors, but the DA said it would take responsibility for correcting inaccurate information originating from the agency.

Immediately after the Senate hearing, Undersecretary for infrastructure and agro-marine logistics Arrey Perez, upon the instruction of Tiu Laurel, met with Kenneth Abante and Dondon Parafina of People’s Budget Coalition and Bisto Proyekto.ph, respectively, together with director Cristy Pilido of the Bureau of Agriculture and Fisheries Engineering to discuss the discrepancies.

At the meeting, the DA and civil society groups identified eight entries out of a total of 1,669 entries or less than one percent with discrepancies in their coordinates which made them off-target from their intended area.
Upon close inspection, it showed that one or two numbers in the coordinate were mistyped.

But the DA and the civil society groups agreed that internal review, cross review and third-party review are necessary to examine the preparation, checking and submission of project documents, identify procedural gaps and propose strengthened internal controls.
The review is administrative in nature and is intended to improve systems and accountability.
The DA at that meeting enlisted the civil society groups to independently check coordinates of FMR projects that were flagged as erroneous.
“We are reviewing the data and working with civil society groups to make sure the technical descriptions are accurate and verifiable,” Laurel said.

“If there are errors in the technical descriptions, whether typographical or otherwise, we will take responsibility and correct them. Public funds must go to the projects they are intended for,” he added.
“This review is not only about correcting individual entries. We are looking at the process itself, so we can close gaps, improve validation and prevent the same errors from recurring.”

Tiu Laurel stressed that Congress retains its constitutional authority over the national budget, while the DA is responsible for ensuring that technical information it submits is accurate and can withstand verification.
The DA will continue coordinating with the House of Representatives, Senate and other concerned agencies as it verifies project descriptions and makes corrections in accordance with budget rules.
Tiu Laurel directed the agency to strengthen geotagging, internal review and third-party validation, including through the FMR Watch portal and citizen monitoring.
The FMR road implementation was recently returned to the DA after more than a decade that it was under the DPWH.
Road Watch portal

Meanwhile, while there were discrepancies pointed out, the civil society groups praised the efforts of the DA in ensuring transparency in the identification and validation of FMR through the FMR Road Watch portal which is currently available to the public.

Through this website, the public can monitor the implementation of the FMRs in their district and across the whole nation with a click of a button. The portal will show the percentage of completion, coordinates and name of the contractor.
They can even upload pictures on the portal of the project itself in-real time. This is a first ever innovation made by the DA since it was handed the implementation of FMR this year.
Perez welcomed this opportunity as transparent measures to ensure public accountability and serve as a multiplier of audit of these kinds of projects.
Further, the Office of the Ombudsman recently preventively suspended several DPWH officials over P94-million ghost FMRs in Davao Occidental.
This is the result of the investigation conducted by the DA over FMRs made during previous years prior.
Tiu Laurel led the filing of the complaints that resulted in the suspensions. Included in the complaint were the private contractors of the projects.
The DA alleged that the projects were declared complete and fully paid for when in truth, actual verification showed little evidence of any work ever being done.

In one case, records showed a project that was reported 100 percent complete was still under construction despite full payment released in 2023. In another, the DA’s Internal Audit Service found no graveled pathways, indicating that the project had not been completed.

articles.title: Move It appeals P555 million penalty
articles.summary: The decision on the rider overboarding case issued against ride-hailing app Move It is not yet final, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board said yesterday.

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — The decision on the rider overboarding case issued against ride-hailing app Move It is not yet final, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board said yesterday.
In a statement, the LTFRB said there is still a pending motion for reconsideration filed by the concerned motorcycle taxi platform provider, noting the legal proceedings are considered still ongoing.
“The LTFRB conducted an investigation on a motorcycle taxi platform provider over allegations that it boarded riders in its online system more than what it is allowed to,” the LTFRB said.

Riders’ group Kapatiran sa Dalawang Gulong (Kagulong) expressed alarm that thousands of motorcycle taxi riders could lose their livelihoods following the decision of the LTFRB against the ride-hailing app.

“Our concern stems from the possibility that, given the enormous amount of the fine, the company might decide to shut down altogether. What will happen to the 73,000 riders whose current livelihood depends on working as motorcycle taxi riders under Move It?” Kagulong secretary general Don Pangan said in a statement.

“Even if Move It continues operating and accepts the ruling, 55,575 riders will still have no assurance that they can continue earning a living. Under the new implementing guidelines, the rider cap will remain in place, limiting the number of riders allowed to operate under Move It to just 17,746,” Pangan said.
Transport group Laban TNVS called out Move It, after several riders were reportedly deactivated following their violation of the rider cap.

“It is truly unfortunate for our fellow Filipinos who, lacking other employment opportunities, have turned to motorcycle taxi driving to make a living – despite the high commissions deducted by the platform and the uncertainty of their daily earnings,” Laban TNVS president Jun de Leon said.

“If the reason for these deactivations is an alleged cap or limit on the number of riders, then removing them from the platform should not be the immediate solution. There ought to be a clear explanation and alternative measures in place so that riders can continue to work, rather than simply being stripped of their source of income,” De Leon added.
Kagulong argued overboarding should not be considered a problem, pointing out in Metro Manila alone, approximately 70 percent of the population relies on public transportation.
According to the group, the current number of operating motorcycle taxi riders is still insufficient to meet the demand for public transportation services.
Kagulong also called for an investigation into other Motorcycle Taxi Platform Providers (MTTPs), as there is a strong possibility that they have also exceeded their respective rider caps.
“We have received reports that JoyRide has also exceeded its rider cap by 10,000, while Angkas has exceeded its limit by 50,000,” Pangan said.

The LTFRB vowed they are focused on addressing the plight of the thousands of overboarded riders “who invested their own resources to earn a decent living – and whose only fault was that they acted in good faith and trusted that they were allowed to operate under the existing rules and regulations.”
Move It responds
Move It general manager Wayne Jacinto addressed the concern of consumers and riders using their app.
“Rides continue, trips continue. Right now, we continue to coordinate with the LTFRB to ensure the protection of the livelihood of our riders,” Jacinto said in a video statement.
He said they have been following the regulatory measures of the LTFRB.
“Move It follows the regulations. Our onboarding mechanisms are based on the real needs of our passengers. What the LTFRB is implementing is the cap which started in 2019,” the general manager said.
“What the regulators are saying is that the cap is static. Which means, what the numbers are, it stays the same,” Jacinto added.
He noted they should also address the ballooning number of passengers using the app, ensuring they are still following the LTFRB’s regulations.
“However, what we believe, along with the other platforms, the cap is the limit of riders that are simultaneously online,” Jacinto said.
“This will ensure that if passengers need more riders, there are enough motorcycles on the road, may it be rush hour or not,” he added.
Jacinto stressed the need for a permanent law for motorcycle taxis to address their concerns.
Pass taxi law
Rep. Ramon Rodrigo Gutierrez of 1-Rider party-list is calling for the immediate passage of the Motorcycle Taxi Bill.
Once enacted, the measure will provide a clear and permanent legal framework for riders.
Gutierrez urged colleagues in the House and the Senate to prioritize the Motorcycle Taxi Bill to protect both the riders and the commuting public. — Delon Porcalla

articles.title: DPWH execs face graft for P491.9 million right-of-way scam
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has filed before the Sandiganbayan graft and malversation charges against six officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH)-Soccsksargen and other…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 12:00am
Department of Public Works and Highways.
Businessworld / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has filed before the Sandiganbayan graft and malversation charges against six officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH)-Soccsksargen and other individuals over an alleged P491.9-million scam involving a road right-of-way in General Santos City.
Personnel of the anti-graft body brought several trolleys carrying stacks of documents as they filed 18 counts of graft and 18 counts of malversation against the accused.
The cases were subsequently raffled to the First, Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Divisions.

In a statement, the ombudsman said it found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction against former DPWH-Soccsksargen regional director Subair Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano San Juan Jr., Tomas Rodriguez, David Padlan, Paisal Padate and Ansare Busran.
Seven private individuals were likewise charged, namely Wilma Mamburam, Nelson Ti, Evelyn Paloso, Rudy Ong, Marisa Seguirre, William Uy and Paul Michael Bagio.

The ombudsman said the charges stemmed from three reports of the National Bureau of Investigation in 2018 and 2019, which involved the payment of right-of-way for 18 parcels of land that were supposedly affected by the construction of the Digos-Makar National Road in Lagao, General Santos City.

The anti-graft body cited a 2017 affidavit of witness Roberto Catapang, who claimed a syndicate, in collusion with the respondent public officials, collected money from the government supposedly as payments for the acquisitions, by fabricating and submitting fake documents.
Through this, the DPWH-Soccsksargen technical working group approved the disbursement of P491.9 million to claimants who were later found to have presented fake documents.
Ombudsman probers also found an alleged unlawful use of a 2009 appraisal value of P3,500 per square meter to determine compensation for properties taken by the government in the early 1990s.
This resulted in “inflated” right-of-way claims, it said.

articles.title: Senate eyes tougher animal welfare law
articles.summary: Senators have called for an inquiry in aid of legislation following a pet crematorium’s alleged dumping of animal remains in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 12:00am

Sen. Pia Cayetano said she would file a resolution to investigate possible animal rights as well as environmental and sanitation violations committed by Bacoor-based Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium.
PAWSsion project
MANILA, Philippines — Senators have called for an inquiry in aid of legislation following a pet crematorium’s alleged dumping of animal remains in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.
Sen. Francis Pangilinan said he would be revising a bill he filed, seeking to amend the 1998 Animal Welfare Act in order to make pet crematoriums accountable for such deed.
Jonathan Legaspi, the pet crematorium’s owner, reportedly could not be held liable under the existing law for an act committed on a dead animal.

Pangilinan recalled the time during the 15th Congress when he helped the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) strengthen the Animal Welfare Act to impose stiffer penalties on animal cruelty and abandonment.

In his Senate Bill 2501 he nicknamed “Dolly’s Act” – named after the aspin in Aklan that survived being scalded with cooking oil – Pangilinan is proposing the creation of an Animal Welfare Bureau under the Department of Agriculture to inspect facilities and ensure the law is implemented with the help of Animal Welfare Enforcement Officers.
“In the final version of the law, we will include facilities like pet crematoriums,” he added.

Pangilinan said even deceased animals deserve dignity after death, as he urged authorities to investigate the crematorium in Bacoor for estafa, breach of contractual obligations under Article 1170 of the Civil Code and local sanitation and solid waste management violations.
Cayetano described the dumping of animal remains “a wanton display of negligence and disdain for the deceased pets.”
“Pets are beloved members of many families. As a pet owner, I understand the grief of losing a pet. A lot of us follow rituals for a proper goodbye,” the senator said.
Sen. JV Ejercito welcomed the Bacoor city government’s move to close the pet crematorium and lead the investigation for criminal charges.
He vowed to support the call for a Senate inquiry on the incident to prevent a repeat of the desecration and to ensure good aftercare services.

“We will look into this matter in aid of legislation to determine what gaps need to be addressed and what measures can be strengthened to prevent similar incidents from happening again,” Ejercito said.
Sen. Joel Villanueva, who hails from Bulacan, lauded the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) for leading a parallel probe.
Villanueva also urged the Department of Environment and Natural Resources and the Department of Trade and Industry to look into solid waste violations and possible business fraud.
Complaints filed
Pet owners yesterday went to the NBI to file complaints against Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium and to have the ashes in their possession verified against the animal remains found in Bulacan.
Members of PAWS and the Animal Kingdom Foundation accompanied the pet owners to the NBI’s Environmental Crime Division.
PAWS executive director Anna Cabrera said the incident had caused severe distress among pet owners.

“We are glad that the NBI invited us because many fur parents have called PAWS in tears. They do not know whether the ashes they have are really those of their fur babies. One of them is even on bed rest because of severe anxiety,” Cabrera said.

AKF president and program director Heidi Marquez-Caguioa said the foundation hoped the NBI investigation would encourage more affected pet owners to come forward. — Mark Ernest Villeza, Ramon Efren Lazaro

articles.title: No shoot-to-kill order vs Bato – PNP
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police has denied issuing a “shoot-to-kill” order for Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, stressing that efforts to arrest the former PNP chief would remain…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police has denied issuing a “shoot-to-kill” order for Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, stressing that efforts to arrest the former PNP chief would remain within the bounds of the law.
PNP spokesman Col. Allen Rae Co said no such order had been issued as he urged the public to rely only on verified information from official sources.
“There is no shoot-to-kill order,” Co said during a briefing at Camp Crame yesterday, reiterating that police would “do everything within the law.”
Co defended the confidentiality of the manhunt, saying operational secrecy was necessary to protect the investigation and those providing information.
He said the PNP is receiving numerous tips about Dela Rosa’s whereabouts and is verifying each one. He declined to disclose details that could compromise the operation.

“That is precisely why we cannot and do not elaborate on what we are doing. These are operations, and we have what we call operational secrecy,” he said, agreeing with Sen. Panfilo Lacson’s remarks that secrecy was key to the operation.
Asked about reports that police had visited residences of people close to the senator, Co said investigators would naturally check places frequented by a wanted person.
Co clarified that a photograph purportedly showing Dela Rosa in a cemetery in Digos City was old.
The PNP’s technical team confirmed that the image was taken three years ago, he said, citing a comment from the person who originally posted it.
The photo showing Dela Rosa claiming to be in the cemetery went viral over the All Saints’ and All Souls’ Day break.
Co warned that people who deliberately spread false information to mislead authorities, obstruct the operation or overwhelm the police hotline could face criminal charges.
He urged the public not to circulate unverified reports, saying the PNP would issue updates on the manhunt at the appropriate time.
Challenge to the DILG, PNP

Malacañang challenged the PNP leadership to disprove notions that law enforcers are finding it hard to arrest Dela Rosa, who was PNP chief when former president Rodrigo Duterte waged his bloody war on drugs.
Dela Rosa has evaded authorities since he escaped from the Senate premises in May.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla admitted in a recent interview that Dela Rosa’s connections as former PNP chief and alumnus of the Philippine Military Academy (PMA) pose difficulties in the efforts to track him.
Speaking to reporters, Palace press officer Claire Castro said the PNP should perform its mandate and enforce the arrest warrant against Dela Rosa, a graduate of PMA “Sinagtala” Class of 1986.

“This is a challenge to the leadership of the DILG and to the leadership of the PNP and the entire police force of our country. Your mandate is to enforce the law, follow the orders given to you in accordance with the Constitution,” Castro said.

“There is a valid warrant of arrest, so it is not for you to decide whether to arrest Sen. Bato dela Rosa, not because he was your chief. This is a challenge to (PNP chief) Gen. (Jose) Nartatez Jr.,” she added.
Castro expressed confidence in the PNP’s capability to carry out its mission under the leadership of Nartatez, also a PMA alumnus.
“We believe in the ability of our police force and we know they will perform the mandate given to them through Gen. Nartatez Jr. That is the impression now, so let us prove them right,” she said.
Castro said President Marcos is not frustrated with the operations against Dela Rosa because law enforcers are continuously searching for the fugitive senator.

The government has offered a P50-million bounty on Dela Rosa. A one-week ultimatum for the senator to surrender expired last Oct. 29. The PNP has created task groups in all 18 regions of the country to find and capture Dela Rosa.
‘Show warrant’
Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte has urged the Marcos administration to make public the arrest warrant against Dela Rosa and assure the public of its validity.
He said authorities should present the document instead of repeatedly hosting press briefings to justify the intended arrest of the senator.
“If there is a valid warrant, then show the warrant,” Duterte said in a statement posted on Facebook.
He accused the government of toying with the law, arguing that authorities should implement the law not only when it’s convenient and in favor of them.
He warned the police against carrying out an arrest without proper legal authority, saying this could constitute kidnapping. — Alexis Romero, Daphne Galvez, Ghio Ong

articles.title: DepEd procures 172,654 MacBooks for teachers
articles.summary: As part of its efforts to accelerate the country’s digital education roadmap, the Department of Education (DepEd) has secured 172,654 Apple MacBook Neo laptops for public school teachers and…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — As part of its efforts to accelerate the country’s digital education roadmap, the Department of Education (DepEd) has secured 172,654 Apple MacBook Neo laptops for public school teachers and administrative staff nationwide.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara announced yesterday that the department had successfully concluded competitive bidding for the computerization project, emphasizing that providing reliable technology would help address long-standing burdens on educators.

“For the longest time, our teachers have carried the heavy personal burden of buying their own laptops or maintaining outdated equipment just to keep up with lesson plans. Under the vision of President Marcos, we are changing the narrative,” Angara said.
The DepEd has so far awarded contracts for 231,725 laptops for teachers nationwide, comprising 169,008 MacBook Neo units and 62,717 Windows-based units.
The procurement also includes 3,646 MacBook Neo laptops for administrative officers.
The deployment of all 172,654 MacBook Neo units is scheduled from November 2026 through March 2027.
DepEd secured the MacBook Neo package at approximately P43,000 per unit, about P6,900 below the model’s Philippine suggested retail price of P49,900.
Angara said the procurement includes a five-year warranty, the longest coverage offered in the department’s laptop procurement, compared with the standard one-year retail warranty.
The package also covers built-in productivity tools, delivery and logistics and professional development for recipients.

“We welcome Apple’s participation in this procurement to bring MacBook Neo to our teachers. It isn’t just about handing out world-class hardware with five-year warranties; it’s about giving our educators the best tools, backed by robust training so they can focus on what matters most: teaching our children,” Angara said.

Apple chief executive officer John Ternus highlighted the deal during the company’s fourth-quarter 2026 financial results conference call on Monday, describing it as Apple’s biggest education deal ever for Mac.

“I’m feeling great about the opportunities ahead for Apple, from our product roadmap and broad range of services to promising areas like health, emerging markets, enterprise and education. As one example, we recently secured our biggest education deal ever for Mac, with the Department of Education in the Philippines. They’re going to deploy 170,000 MacBook Neos to teachers and staff,” Ternus said.
DepEd will also collaborate with Apple to launch GuroXL, a co-designed training framework for educators.

In coordination with the National Educators Academy of the Philippines, the program will guide teachers toward Apple Teacher certifications and specialized technology leadership credentials, according to the department.
ACT: Insufficient
The Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) Philippines, however, said the 172,654 laptops remain grossly insufficient to meet the digital needs of the entire public education workforce.

ACT chairperson Ruby Bernardo explained that with nearly 900,000 public school teachers alone, the latest procurement, even when combined with previously contracted units, would leave the vast majority of teachers without government-provided laptops.

While ACT recognizes the need to equip educators with reliable digital tools, she stressed that the procurement must not be presented as fulfilling the government’s promise to provide every teacher with a laptop.

“Our educators are subsidizing the government’s failure to provide even the most basic tools for their work. It is deeply unjust that those already burdened by low salaries, excessive workloads and inadequate benefits must also go into debt just to do their jobs,” she added.
Bernardo called on the DepEd to ensure that the laptops are reasonably priced, fully functional, durable and suited to the actual working requirements of teachers and administrative personnel.
She also urged the department to provide accessible and continuing training, along with reliable technical support and maintenance.

“Schools should not be forced to raffle off a handful of devices or its personnel to compete for limited units when these are essential tools for their work. Our demand remains clear: laptop for every teacher and public funds that actually reach schools and education workers,” said Bernardo.

articles.title: ICC bars use of Tagalog for opening statements
articles.summary: Trial judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have prohibited lawyers representing drug war victims from using Tagalog in their opening statement during the upcoming trial of former…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 12:00am
Former president Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court in The Hague in this file photo from Sept. 16 this year, during a preparatory session.
ICC

MANILA, Philippines — Trial judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have prohibited lawyers representing drug war victims from using Tagalog in their opening statement during the upcoming trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte for crimes against humanity.

During Monday’s status conference, Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner denied the request of the common legal representatives of the victims to partly use Tagalog in their opening statements.

“The Rome Statute is quite clear. The working languages of the court are English and French,” Korner said. “There has to be a really exceptional reason why a language that is not one of the court languages should be used.”

Paolina Massidda, principal counsel at ICC’s Office of Public Counsel for Victims, said they wanted to use Tagalog in their opening statement to relay the specific remarks made by some of the victims in the case.
“A lot of victims will be connecting to the hearing. For them, it would be important to listen how we convey to the chamber what they narrated to us, their experiences,” Massidda said.
“They will connect much more if that is done in Tagalog. It’s a very limited request for this purpose,” she added.
While they understand the purpose of the request, Korner said the court is inclined to follow the rule on the official languages for the conduct of the hearing.
“There are going to be interpreters,” the judge said. “While we understand that you want the victims to relate to what’s being said, all of it, everything you say… will be translated in any event.”
The ruling is so far limited to the use of Tagalog for the opening statements. It remains unclear if there would be witnesses who would testify in Philippine languages.
The ICC earlier released a job posting for Tagalog and Cebuano translators, who would serve as paraprofessional interpreters and associate court interpreters.

articles.title: ICC prosecutors cite 'fabricated' PNP drug war accounts in testimony bid
articles.summary: International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors ask Trial Chamber III to admit another set of prior recorded testimonies of witnesses against former President Rodrigo Duterte - this time, those who…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: Published November 3, 2026 11:33pm

PRAGUE, Czech Republic – International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors ask Trial Chamber III to admit another set of prior recorded testimonies of witnesses against former President Rodrigo Duterte – this time, those who provide proof of the alleged pattern of crimes during his administration’s drug war.

In their sixth request, released publicly on November 2, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang noted that the prior recorded testimonies of witnesses P-1136, P-1345, P-1391, and P-1404, if admitted in court, would cut direct examination time from 16 hours to four hours.
As with previous applications, the prosecution seeks to apply ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence Rule 68(3) for this batch of witnesses.

If Trial Chamber III approves, this witness batch would have their prior recorded statements admitted in court, alongside their court appearance for “focused supplementary questioning”. They would also remain available for cross-examination by Duterte’s defense.
Prior recorded testimonies of four witnesses

The prosecution stated that P-1136, P-1345, P-1391, and P-1404 provide evidence on violence in the Philippines before and during Duterte’s presidency, including the targeting of alleged drug personalities, the use of watchlists, and alleged efforts to conceal or justify killings.

The prosecution also said the four accounts establish a policy to “neutralise” alleged criminals through violent crimes, including murder, as well as the alleged widespread and systematic character of crimes committed during the drug war.

P-1136’s statement indicates that Duterte allegedly targeted public officials considered “high-value targets” over suspected involvement in illegal drugs, with some allegedly appearing on the so-called “PRRD List”. Prosecutors said the testimony goes to their allegation that Duterte had a policy to “neutralise” local officials allegedly linked to the illegal drug trade.

For P-1345, the prosecutors said the statement is evidence of a “new pattern of killings during ‘One Time Big Time’ operations” in Manila after Duterte became president. The witness discussed nine case files involving PNP killings of alleged drug personalities and identified an alleged pattern that included planting shabu and guns near victims’ bodies. The witness also said journalists, human rights groups, labor leaders and judges who opposed the Duterte administration were “red-tagged” as drug personalities or communists.

P-1391’s evidence, the prosecutors stated, is on the use of drug watchlists, patterns of “fabricated Philippine National Police (PNP) accounts of killings,” the alleged use of paid assets by police to carry out killings, and rewards allegedly received by PNP officers as incentives. The witness also provides evidence relating to Incidents 21 and 30 in the prosecution’s case.

The prosecution also said P-1404’s testimony is evidence of barangay clearance operations and different types of drug watchlists, including PDEA, barangay, PNP, and presidential lists. Prosecutors said the witness described how barangay captains were allegedly ordered through the Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) to submit updated watchlists every month. P-1404 also provides evidence on the aftermath of the killing of Kian delos Santos, identified as Incident 30, and on reports in which killings were presented as “accomplishments.”
Pending decision
If the Chamber grants the application, prosecutors are asking for around one hour of supplementary examination for each witness instead of an estimated four hours of direct examination per witness.

This would save “at least 12 hours of court time,” the prosecutors argued, adding that such testimonies would not prejudice Duterte because the defense would still have “ample opportunity to cross-examine” all four witnesses.
P-1136, P-1345, P-1391, and P-1404 would also be asked at the start of their testimony whether they consent to having their earlier statements introduced into the trial record.
The filing comes a day after Trial Chamber III held a status conference as the ICC enters the final weeks of preparations for Duterte’s trial.
Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed during his terms as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.
His trial is scheduled to open on November 30 before Trial Chamber III, composed of Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: China tells Philippines to stop politicians crossing 'red lines'
articles.summary: Beijing, China—China’s top diplomat Wang Yi urged the Philippines on Tuesday to rein in politicians who had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing and crossed its “red lines”. The…

blocks.text: Beijing, China—China’s top diplomat Wang Yi urged the Philippines on Tuesday to rein in politicians who had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing and crossed its “red lines”. articles.title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’
articles.summary: A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final…

blocks.text: It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote, Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.

Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.

Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.

blocks.caption: An intimate glimpse … one of Tagore’s unseen artwork on display. Photograph: Christie’s Images Ltd 2026

blocks.text: The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.
I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.

One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.

For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.
“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.

“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.

blocks.caption: Window to a master’s practice … A manuscript by Rabindranath Tagore, on display at Christie’s. Photograph: Christie’s Images Ltd 2026

blocks.text: Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.

“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.

There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.

Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.
On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.
Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.

He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”
Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.

blocks.caption: A voyage through another time … Malvika Singh’s Cooking for my Firefly. Photograph: Handout

blocks.text: Freddy Birdy, a copywriter whose delightful words have earned him a devoted Instagram following, recommends writer and historian Malvika Singh’s cookbook, Cooking for My Firefly.

“This book isn’t about recipes, though it does include them. It is a voyage through another time and place, tracing the social fabric of India of the 60s, 70s and 80s, trickling down to today. Told in Malvika’s beautiful prose, it takes us to a time when people entertained in homes, not in restaurants; when dishes were cooked in-house and there were no caterers or party planners. An era long before Instagram posts, WhatsApp invitations, celebrity chefs and food delivery apps, when the point of having a party was simply to have fun. It is an archive of photographs, food, culture, gossip, movie stars, politicians, royalty, set against the spectacular backdrop of Malvika’s dining tables through the decades. I like to dip into it every now and then, much as one might do standing in a dark kitchen with the light of the refrigerator enticing you to midnight goodies.”

blocks.text: At a time when public anger has spilled into the streets, artist Aamir Aziz’s new track, Dopeher Blues (Afternoon Blues), captures the frustration and angst of a generation that has lived through many crises.

Aziz describes the song as an expression of a period of deep suffocation. Issues such as farmer suicides, unemployment and conflicts in Palestine and Kashmir, he told me, are things he has grown up with even as public attention shifts with the news cycle. It is also a warning, in part, against internet culture, where injustices risk becoming normalised.

Aziz, 35, works in acting, music and writing, and became an internet sensation with his defiant poem Sab Yaad Rakha Jayega (Everything Will Be Remembered) during the citizenship protests. At the heart of his new track is a note of defiance and hope: “We’ll find a way to sing,” he says, as he calls on everyone “to keep speaking up even in a climate of fear, misinformation and oppression.”

articles.title: Americans head to polls in midterm elections seen as referendum on Trump
articles.summary: Control of the Senate and House of Representatives, both currently held by the Republicans, is at stake
articles.byline: Robert Tait in Yarmouth, Maine, Joseph Gedeon in Detroit, Michigan, and Rachel Leingang in Waverly, Iowa

blocks.text: Americans are heading to the polls today in US midterm elections widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump’s second presidency and a chance for opponents to rein in his untrammeled power.

Democrats and Republicans have scrambled in recent days to deliver their final pitches to voters, with control of the US Senate and House of Representatives – both currently held by the Republicans – at stake. Also on the ballot are 36 governor’s races, as well as control of state legislatures, sheriffs races and ballot measures.

The campaign has been overshadowed by Trump, who has staged several dozen rallies across the country while urging his make America great again (Maga) base to vote for Republican candidates and pretend his name was on the ballot.

The party holding the White House typically loses congressional seats at midterm elections, and Democrats are hoping Trump’s nose-diving popularity can be exploited to generate a “blue wave” groundswell of popular opposition that will win them the Senate and the House.

They are seeking to wrest control over both chambers of Congress to put a brake on Trump’s presidential power, which has gone largely unchecked as he launched a fierce immigration crackdown involving mass arrests and deportations, waged war on Iran, imposed tariffs on foreign imports and embarked on vainglorious building projects, including a White House ballroom.

Opinion surveys have suggested the Democrats are well positioned to win the House. The party faces a tougher task to regain control of the Senate, although it has targeted several Republican-held seats including Ohio, Texas and Maine.

“There has to be a better way for everyday people to be able to live their lives out here,” said Maine’s Democratic senate candidate Troy Jackson in final pitch to voters on Monday. “And if we quit wasting money on foreign wars, if we quit giving money to billionaires, if we quit doing these dumbass tariffs and things like that, we can make people’s lives better by prioritizing what we want to do in this country to help regular, everyday people, and that’s what this race is about. I’m tired of watching elected officials cater to people like Elon Musk.”

blocks.caption: Volunteers hand out signs for the Democratic candidate James Talarico at his final campaign rally in Austin, Texas, on Monday. Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

blocks.text: A final set of polls from the New York Times and Siena University, published on Sunday, put Democratic candidates ahead in five of seven key battleground contests – including Texas and Kansas, where voters have not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988 and 1932 respectively.

The final stretch of the campaign was not without drama for the Democrats, however. In Michigan – widely seen as a crucial pillar to either party’s ambitions of control in the Senate – the Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost her party’s senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, on Sunday.

Stevens was widely condemned by fellow Democrats over the move, which followed a feud with the El-Sayed campaign over an outside group’s campaign ad that blamed the high cost of living on US support for Israel. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, described her endorsement of Rogers as “a despicable betrayal”.
“Whatever they’re trying to distract you, it’s because they’re picking your pocket,” El-Sayed told hundreds of supporters in Royal Oak, Michigan on Monday.

The extraordinary rupture took places days after the party faced damaging headlines in Alaska, where it was reported that the Democratic senate candidate’s campaign was behind an effort to recruit a challenger with almost the same name as her rival, the Republican senator Dan Sullivan. (The Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, has denied any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign.)

Before the report of the Peltola campaign’s involvement, the Department of Justice (DoJ) filed a lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s Senate results in the event of a Republican defeat, citing potential “voter confusion” over the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. The lawsuit has since been dismissed by a judge.

Trump has put himself center stage by crisscrossing the country to deliver a succession of speeches for Republican candidate, despite opinion polls showing his approval ratings falling to record lows of between 33 and 37%.

In his final public campaign appearance on Monday, Trump spent most of the time in a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington’s reflecting Pool. “This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said, 26 minutes into the speech, before quickly returning to talking about renovations. Schumer called it a “pathetic closing message”.

blocks.caption: These midterms are widely seen as a referendum on Donald Trump’s second presidency. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters

blocks.text: Democrats have sought to reinforce the message that the election is about Trump while trying to highlight the perceived corruption of the US president and his family, along with affordability issues and the impact of the conflict with Iran, which is seen as having exacerbated the cost of living.

Opinion surveys have shown that voters have become increasingly concerned about corruption in government. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that 76% think elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people.
Disclosures to the US office of government ethics show that Trump has made about $2.2bn since returning to the White House, including royalties from his own name-branded meme coin.
As the president has grown wealthier, voters have chafed under rising living costs, which Trump vowed to reduce during his 2024 presidential campaign.

The war with Iran – which Trump launched in February in tandem with Israel – has stoked inflation by increasing global oil prices, which has led to higher prices at the pump for American motorists and raised the cost of diesel, a vital fuel for supply chains and farmers.

“We need to focus that anger and point it at where it ought to be pointed, which is at a broken two-choice political system that is too easily abused to allow elected officials to be corrupt and to be lazy and still hold power,” Rob Sand, Iowa’s Democratic candidate for governor, said on Monday.
The US elections also take place under a shadow of uncertainty about whether Trump will accept the results if they do not go the Republicans’ way.

Alaska is just one of the cases being pursued by the justice department – under the control of Trump’s close ally, Todd Blanche, the attorney general – that opponents say are designed to cast doubt on the election’s integrity, including through baseless claims of mass voting by non-US citizens.
The department plans to deploy a record 1,000 election monitors to polling stations across the US. Critics have denounced the move as voter intimidation.

articles.title: Why South Africa's local elections matter
articles.summary: South Africans head to the polls on Wednesday amid water shortages, frustration with local services and questions over whether the ANC's support will keep falling.

image.caption: Water shortages ‌and unreliable electricity ⁠supplies ⁠have become symbols of municipal failures that have angered votersImage: Themba Hadebe/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We've decided not to vote. At all," said Vatiswa Zoya, two days before voters in South Africa cast their ballots for new municipal government leaders. "What is the point? We will still sleep hungry."
These very same frustrations are what will lead 22-year-old Lindokuhle Mbandazayo to the polls, although she has yet to decide where to place her cross.

"When we vote for councilors, we ask them to fix the area," Mbandazayo told DW. "The electricity goes off regularly here. There is also sewage in the streets and we have to jump over this. There are a lot of things that need to be fixed here."

Both women live in Tembisa, a township in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city. Both express an "embedded frustration" over their living conditions.

blocks.caption: Many voters will be asking whether they'll have water to shower on election day, as shortages persistImage: Siphiwe Sibeko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, noted that it is this "embedded frustration" that prompts people to vote.
"Your vote actually puts some of these political parties' feet to the fire, but I think that frustration is also inherently coming from the fact that it's not going to happen overnight," Naidu said.

On Wednesday, South Africans will vote in local government elections that will determine control of the country's largest cities and test whether the African National Congress (ANC), the leading party in a national government coalition, continues its electoral decline.
Here are five things to know about the November 4 election.
1. Water as a key voter issue
Many voters will be motivated by whether they can shower or not on voting day, as many parts of the country experience water supply issues.
In Johannesburg, several neighborhoods have faced water cuts and rationing for weeks as old infrastructure struggles to keep up with supply.

"Every province has an issue. So if we take for example drinking water quality, half of the drinking water systems in South Africa are not fit for drinking," said Ferrial Adam, executive director of water rights NGO WaterCAN.

"Almost 70% of our wastewater treatment works are in a critical state and spewing sewage into rivers and streams across the country," she told DW during a protest over water cuts in Johannesburg, adding that "it is a definite water crisis across South Africa."
In Tshwane, a metropolitan area that includes South Africa's administrative capital, Pretoria, a recent water treatment failure left more than 400 residents sick.

Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, says that despite widespread worries about water quality and supply, many of those campaigning have not provided adequate details on their solutions.

"I think their promises have been very transactional. Their promises are always, you know, we're going to bring water to your community. We're going to make sure the taps are flowing. We're going to ensure that we're going to deal with the old infrastructure around water, etc. But I don't think they've dug deeper in terms of understanding what the budgets say about water access," she said.
2. ANC in decline
Many voters place blame for the state of municipalities on the African National Congress, which has historically held an outright majority in most municipalities.

In 2016 the ANC secured 53.91% of the overall vote and had an outright majority in 161 of 213 councils. In 2021, that decreased to 45.59% of the overall vote with a majority in 122 of 213 municipalities.
Global marketing research firm Ipsos predicts that the party's support could fall as low as 30% in this election, resulting in an increase in coalition-run municipalities.
South Africa sees nationwide protests over migrants
Naidu notes that the party has struggled to keep up with the expectations of evolving voters, particularly millennial and Gen Zvoters who now make up the bulk of voters.
"You have an electorate that wants to see who are these people that you're putting out there to say you're going to make things work for us," she said.
Mbandazayo is one such voter, who is casting her ballot in her second election and says she is looking for a new voice in politics.
"We need change. I am considering voting for another party because the current party is not doing well for us because we've been voting for them for a long time," she told DW.
3. Migration a big talking point
South Africa has seen a wave of protests around migration for several months, ramping up in October with opposition to the country's asylum process.
Murmur Intelligence, a digital analysis firm, says parties including Action SA, the MK Party and the Patriotic Alliance have used immigration as a campaign issue.
"The party that might claim the most benefit from that sentiment … is Action SA, noted Murmur Intelligence co-founder Aldu Cornelissen.

"They would make a clear argument that we need to get rid of illegal immigrants. We need to improve immigration. We need to protect our borders, which are all legitimate concerns, right? So, if any of the parties could capitalize on this sentiment, it would be them."
"But for what percentage? I would wager between 6% and 8%, roughly," Cornelissen added.
Those margins may seem low, but in an increasingly fractured political landscape parties are fighting for every vote.

The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has said 136,760 candidates are contesting across the country, with 75 parties contesting in Johannesburg, 70 in Tshwane and 69 in eThekwini (Durban and surrounding areas).
4. Election misinformation

Fake news and false AI-generated content have become a feature in this election, with the IEC investigating over 700 complaints of disinformation. One of the prominent claims has been an accusation that the ANC plans to mobilize asylum seekers to vote for them.
Asylum seekers, refugees and permanent residents can't legally vote in South African elections regardless of how long they've been in the country.
South Africa election hit by disinformation surge

William Bird, director of media monitoring agency Moxii Africa, says misinformation and disinformation "are now kind of part and parcel of your standard build-up to any electoral environment, wherever you are in the world."

"What we see with disinformation is that it always picks up on whatever the hot button news issues are, as well as the standard kind of tropes about elections, he said, adding that there's always going to be "some bunch of clowns" saying the elections are rigged.

"And in South Africa's case, there's no evidence to support that at all. The IEC [Electoral Commission of South Africa] is one of the best electoral management bodies in the world. So of course, you then see people that are either wanting to destabilize, or they're wanting to just shake things up and make people scared or angry, and so they use those kinds of narratives. And that, unfortunately, is becoming an increasingly common trait," Bird told DW.
Bird added that social media platforms often "incentivize and deliberately encourage people" to attack others online.
5. Will people make it to the polls?

Local government election turnout has historically been lower than turnout in national elections. In 2016, turnout was at 57.95% and dropped to 45.87%. In 2024, in the most recent national elections, turnout was at 58.64%.
Naidu says this election will ultimately depend less on online discussions or campaign slogans and more on how many people make it to the polls.
Voters will mark two ballots — one for a direct local representative and a second for a political party under a proportional representation (PR) system.
Seats allocated through the PR vote account for half of all council seats, making them as important as the direct votes for councilors and this is where voter turnout becomes a key element.

"That is why political parties are saying to people, go out and vote, go out and vote, because if you don't go out and vote, it has an impact on the calculation of what you win as a PR vote in the council and the seats that you get," she said. In turn, this affects the make-up of each municipality and whether new coalition governments will form.
Could you still afford to live in Cape Town today?
Additional reporting by Ahmed Kajee and Sofia Christensen

articles.title: Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
articles.summary: Rio Tinto is jointly funding a A$28m "toad containment zoe" to protect the Pilbara region.

blocks.text: Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation.
The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.
While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.
Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.
The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.
Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.
"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."
The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.
In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.
If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.
The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.
A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.
The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.

articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin, and emphasized Europe needs to be included in any peace talks with Russia. At the same time, Merz doubts Moscow is serious…

image.caption: Zelenskyy arrived hours after Russian strikes hit Ukraine, with air defense and energy support key themes in his talks with MerzImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Tuesday he had seen no sign that Russia was serious about negotiating a ceasefire in Ukraine, speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin.
Both leaders said Europe must help shape any lasting peace.
Germany expects European representatives to be in Abu Dhabi for next week's US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia, though they are unlikely to have a seat at the table.

"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," Merz said when asked about the Abu Dhabi talks. "I do not see that happening so far."

Zelenskyy said he hopes the Abu Dhabi talks, the first trilateral sit down since February, could pave the way for a direct meeting between the Ukrainian president and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who has thus far refused several offers from Zelenskyy for face-to-face talks.
"We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders," he told reporters.
Europe must have a say on postwar security
Merz said Europe must have a say on sanctions and postwar security.

He said the local ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a model for a wider truce, but warned that Russian attacks in the Black Sea risked further escalation. "Russia is precipitating a global food crisis, to the detriment of the poorest nations and countries in the world," he said.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine wanted a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain shipments through the Black Sea and further prisoner exchanges.
Lavrov sets conditions for talks with Zelenskyy at G20 meeting

The Ukrainian president said a ceasefire alone would not secure a lasting peace. Ukraine would need security guarantees backed by Europe and the US. He insisted Europe must be involved in the negotiations.
"There cannot be a sustainable peace if Europe is not at the negotiating table," Zelenskyy said.
He said Ukraine would join the US, European partners and NATO for talks on security guarantees and reconstruction in Brussels on Wednesday.
Russia increases attacks on Ukrainian civilians
The talks in Berlin come as Russia continues to increase airstrikes on Ukrainian civilians.

Zelenskyy said at least 33 people were killed, and more than 50 could be trapped in rubble, after multiple Russian strikes on a school building used as an aid distribution center in the frontline southeastern village of on Monday.

Ukrainian officials said Russian forces launched an initial strike on residents waiting to receive aid, and then hit the same location again after waiting for rescue personnel to arrive on the scene, killing several of them and destroying emergency vehicles.
Speaking in Berlin, Zelenskyy described the strike as "one of the largest Russian killings of this war."
On Tuesday, at least 73 people were injured in a strike on a hospital in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, and 226 patients had to be transferred to other hospitals, regional prosecutors said.

blocks.caption: Russian forces struck the aid center twice after waiting for rescue workers to arriveImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Germany pledges aid ahead of winter
"Ahead of the next winter, air defense and the energy sector are our priorities," Merz said. He said Germany would soon deliver new aid in both areas and provide further winter assistance this year.
Zelenskyy thanked Germany for helping protect Ukraine's skies and supporting its energy infrastructure.
"Without Germany, we would not be as strong as we are," he said.
He said Ukraine urgently needed more air defense equipment, including Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy told EU leaders in October that Ukraine would need an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) from European governments next year. Germany plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine in mid-November to discuss further support ahead of winter.
How has Berlin stepped up security?
The visit coincides with the opening of the two-day Berlin Security Conference, which brings together European officials and defense experts. Russia's war in Ukraine is high on the agenda.
Police said about 3,400 additional officers were deployed for the visit and the conference, with reinforcements from across Germany.

Armed officers guarded barriers around parts of the government district, and special police units deployed snipers. Roads were also closed in western Berlin, including near the Kurfürstendamm shopping avenue.

articles.title: Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes
articles.summary: The US company was named after the Greek goddess of victory, so the Dar al-Ifta said displaying its logo was unIslamic.

blocks.text: Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.
The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.
It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.
Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.
The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.

It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.
The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.
The BBC has contacted Nike for comment.

The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.

Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.
The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.
Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.
The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.
In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.
The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.
The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.
Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.
Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.
In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

articles.title: China and India achieved diplomatic thaw. Now the border is flaring up
articles.summary: Indian authorities have confirmed a new border "face-off" between Indian and Chinese troops in Arunachal Pradesh, raising questions about the still fragile thaw in relations between New Delhi and…

image.caption: The de facto border between India and China runs through a remote mountainous areaImage: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur sounded alarm bells across India by confirming that Indian and Chinese troops had confronted each other at several locations along the de facto border in Arunachal Pradesh state, in India's northeast.
"In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened (with Chinese troops) at various locations in Arunachal and it still continues," he told reporters last month.
"It may be difficult to counter China by conventional means because their PLA and BDR (Border Defense Regiment) have gone way ahead with investment and modernization," he said.
The disputed China-India border runs through a remote mountainous region.
Throughout the decades, clashes along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border, have repeatedly triggered security crises between the world's two most populous nations.
Ties between Beijing and New Delhi are still affected by the deadly violence in 2020, when both countries accused each other of trying to seize territory.

In June that year, a clash in the Galwan River valley in eastern Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops, according to Indian sources. China later confirmed four of its soldiers died.
Arunachal Pradesh leader Pema Khandu says situation normal

Kapur's remarks have brought renewed attention to the Himalayan frontier. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has acknowledged but also downplayed the border transgressions, saying such incidents were not new and the situation along the border was normal.
Khandu acknowledged that the border was not properly demarcated and that China did not recognize the McMahon Line, drawn by the British Empire in 1914, which separates Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet.
It was also not clear if the latest confrontations between the Chinese and Indian troops involved physical violence.
Tracking the tense relationship between India and China
China rejects wrongdoing

The opposition Congress party criticized Khandu's remarks, and accused the ruling BJP, led by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, of "rationalizing" Chinese actions instead of asserting India's position.

"On this there has been a deafening silence from the PM and his establishment," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said in a post on X, referring to the face-offs confirmed by the border police chief.
Meanwhile, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal attributed the incidents to Chinese forces changing up their patrol routes.
"As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," he said.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations, saying Chinese troops were conducting "normal patrols" and strictly abiding by bilateral agreements.
Why do face-offs keep happening?
The LAC largely separates Indian- and Chinese-controlled territory. However, as forces from both nations patrol territory they regard as their own, they sometimes venture into disputed areas.
"There is a very simple reason — because there is no agreed line between the two," Gautam Bambawale, a former Indian ambassador to China, told DW.

The de-facto border stretches for 3,488 kilometres (2,167 miles) according to India, but China claims it is shorter. The two countries have held 25 rounds of talks between their Special Representatives since 2003, but have yet to reach a boundary settlement.
The dispute is particularly sensitive in Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as part of southern Tibet.
Finding home in exile: Tibetans in India resist China
China building a hydropower dam in Tibet
Aravind Yelery, a China expert at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the region has become more strategically important to Beijing.
"Both sides patrol a contested LAC, so friction is built into the arrangement," Yelery told DW.

"What is new is China's intensified focus on the eastern sector. Since announcing the 60,000-megawatt Medog hydropower project in Tibet, Beijing has poured infrastructure, troops, engineers and machinery into the area."
South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere

He described the LAC as "not a thin line but a deep zone of overlapping claims where patrols inevitably meet." Face-offs will continue, he argued, until diplomacy produces concrete arrangements on the ground.
According to Yelery, the diplomatic pledges made by Indian and Chinese leaders will take time to implement.
"A wide gap separates the leaders' promises from the measures that would prevent a repeat of 2020, namely disengagement and mutual restraint," he added.
What is different about the latest developments?
For India, the immediate concern is whether the recent encounters reflect familiar patrol disputes or a more significant change in Chinese activity along the frontier.
Ashok Kantha, another former Indian ambassador to China, said Chinese transgressions in the eastern sector were not new, but that their location and extent mattered.
"If the Chinese have now made deeper intrusions on our side of the LAC, or established a presence in new areas, or expanded their existing presence, that would be a serious development," he added.
He also pointed to agreements signed by the two countries to maintain peace along the border.

"Any such transgression would be in complete violation of several border-related agreements India and China have signed (1993, 1996, 2005, 2012 and 2013). In these, both sides committed to respect and strictly observe the LAC, and not to alter the status quo."
The Indian government has not publicly provided details of the locations or circumstances of the latest face-offs, making it unclear whether they have changed the situation on the ground.
A fragile diplomatic thaw

The renewed encounters come as India and China try to stabilize relations and move past the 2020 clashes. Both Beijing and New Delhi made reconciliatory moves, including restoring some direct flights and easing restrictions on travel and economic exchanges.

The diplomatic reset gathered pace after Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping met at the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024. They met again at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025 and at the BRICS summit in New Delhi this year.
The boundary dispute, however, remains unresolved.
India builds tunnel in Himalayas to counter China threat
Alka Acharya, director of the Institute of Chinese Studies in New Delhi, cautioned against drawing conclusions about the latest encounters without more information.
The government has described the incidents as face-offs, she said, but has not indicated that Chinese troops have taken control of Indian territory.

"The question is what is the nature of the so-called 'clashes' … not why the clashes are happening again? Any opinion on this latest kerfuffle would at best be conjecture without any definitive evidence," Acharya told DW.

Border incidents have occurred regularly over the past decade and a half, despite political and diplomatic negotiations. The unresolved dispute, she added, will continue to sustain distrust and constrain the broader relationship.
Whether the latest encounters signal a more serious escalation will depend on details that New Delhi has yet to make public.

articles.title: Trump claims U.S. will halt $4B funding to Israel at end of 2026
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in funding to Israel after the end of this year.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after a meeting in Palm Beach, Fla., in this Dec. 29, 2025, file photo. Speaking to Fox News's Fox and Friends on Tuesday, Trump said he made a deal with Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in fund

blocks.text: World·New
U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in funding to Israel after the end of this year.
No immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on U.S. president's remarks
U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion US in funding to Israel after the end of this year.

Speaking to Fox News's Fox and Friends, Trump said Israel no longer needed the funding and that some Democrats and left-wing politicians were using the U.S. financial support to Israel as a talking point to criticize Republicans.
"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump said.
"We've already agreed that by the end of this year, we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it."
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on Trump's remarks.

items: A new progressive wave is exposing the Democratic rift over Israel — just the way Republicans want it
Lack of big-name Democratic candidates at pro-Israel conference confirms for some voters the party has changed

blocks.text: It was not immediately clear which exact funding Trump was referring to. A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annually in U.S. military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028, and conversations have been under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
"They can buy whatever they want. They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," Trump added in his comments Tuesday.

Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off U.S. military support within a decade. In a June letter to a U.S. ​congressman, he wrote that the time had come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."

U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48 per cent of voters and 66 per cent of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 per cent and 20 per cent when the question was first asked in 2017.

Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of U.S. support for Israel.
"The left uses the $4-billion payment that everybody knows about — well, it's no secret — as a signal of unfairness, and we can't allow that to happen," Trump said.
"We were giving them $4 billion, we are. But it gets cut off at the end of the year," he said. "Why? Because they don't need it."
